details:
**Finn MacCool (Fionn mac Cumhaill) and the Salmon of Knowledge**
Finn is the leader of the Fianna, a band of warriors, and the central hero of the Fenian Cycle of Irish myth. As a boy he cooked the Salmon of Knowledge for the poet Finn Eces, who had spent seven years trying to catch it. When Finn burned his thumb on the fish and sucked it, he gained all the world's knowledge, and afterward he could call up wisdom by sucking his thumb. Legend says he sleeps beneath Ireland until the hour of its need.

**Cu Chulainn and the Gae Bulg**
Cu Chulainn is the great hero of the Ulster Cycle. He learned warfare, including the "salmon leap," from the warrior woman Scathach, who gave him the barbed spear Gae Bulg, which inflicts wounds that cannot be survived. He used it to kill his foster-brother Ferdiad and, without knowing who he was, his own son Connla.

**The Cattle Raid of Cooley (Tain Bo Cuailnge) and Queen Medb**
The central epic of the Ulster Cycle. Queen Medb (Maeve) of Connacht invaded Ulster to steal the prized Brown Bull of Cooley. While the men of Ulster lay weakened by a curse, the teenage Cu Chulainn held off her armies alone, fighting champions one by one at a river ford. In battle he went into the riastrad, a monstrous "warp spasm" or battle frenzy.

**Oisin and Tir na nOg**
Oisin (Ossian) is Finn's son, a poet who narrates much of the Fenian Cycle. He went with the fairy woman Niamh on the magical horse Enbarr, which could cross the sea, to Tir na nOg, the "Land of the Young." When he returned to Ireland, he touched the ground (dismounted or fell from the horse) and at once aged the 300 years that had passed. Irish myth also includes other otherworld paradises, such as Mag Mell, and the immram genre of voyages to magical islands.

**Diarmuid and Grainne**
Grainne, daughter of the High King Cormac mac Airt, was engaged to the aging Finn MacCool but eloped with the young warrior Diarmuid Ua Duibhne, whose "love spot" on his forehead made any woman who saw it fall in love with him. Finn chased them for years, and when Diarmuid was gored by a boar, Finn let him die by twice letting the healing water drain from his hands.

**Sadhbh, the deer woman**
Sadhbh was Finn's wife, who had been turned into a deer by a druid. Finn's hounds Bran and Sceolan recognized her and refused to kill her. She became a woman again on Finn's land and gave birth to Oisin, whose name means "little deer."

**The Morrigan**
The shape-shifting Irish goddess of war, fate, and death, often appearing as a crow. She is often described as a triple goddess made up of Badb, Macha, and Nemain. She clashed with Cu Chulainn during the Tain, partly over a cow, and her crow perched on his shoulder when he died. She is also linked to the festival of Samhain.

**Lebor Gabala Erenn (The Book of Invasions)**
A medieval pseudo-history describing successive waves of settlers in Ireland: Cessair (a granddaughter of Noah, with Ladra), then Partholon, Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the Tuatha De Danann, and finally the Milesians (Gaels). The early settlers fought the Fomorians, a monstrous race whose leader Cichol Gricenchos fought the first battle in Ireland. When the Milesians arrived, the goddess Eriu asked that the island be named after her, which gives the name Eire.

**Battles of Mag Tuired, Nuada's silver arm, and Lugh vs. Balor**
In the first Battle of Mag Tuired ("Plain of Pillars"), the Tuatha De Danann defeated the Fir Bolg, but their king Nuada lost his arm to Sreng. Because a king had to be physically whole, Nuada could not rule until he was given a silver arm (Airgetlam). In the second battle, against the Fomorians, Balor of the Evil Eye, whose eye destroyed whatever it looked at, killed Nuada. His own grandson Lugh of the Long Arm then shot a stone from his sling through that eye, so the eye's gaze turned on and destroyed the Fomorian army.

**Tuatha De Danann: the Dagda and the craft gods**
The Tuatha De Danann are the divine race of Irish myth, told in the Mythological Cycle. The Dagda, their father-figure god, owned a club that killed with one end and brought back to life with the other, and a cauldron that never emptied. The three craft gods are Goibniu the smith, Luchta the carpenter (wright), and Creidhne the metalworker (goldsmith), who made weapons together for the second Battle of Mag Tuired.

**The Lia Fail and the Hill of Tara**
The Lia Fail ("Stone of Destiny") stood on the Hill of Tara, the seat of the High Kings of Ireland. It was said to roar with joy when the rightful king touched it. It was one of the four treasures the Tuatha De Danann brought to Ireland.

**Geis and the death of Cu Chulainn**
A geis is a magical taboo or obligation laid on an Irish hero. Cu Chulainn ("Hound of Culann") had a geis against eating dog meat and another against refusing hospitality. Three hags offered him dog meat, which forced him to break one of them, and the weakened hero was killed by Lugaid. He tied himself to a standing stone so he could die on his feet.

**The Children of Lir**
The four children of Lir were turned into swans by their jealous stepmother Aoife and doomed to spend 900 years on Irish waters. The spell was broken when they heard the bell of a Christian church, after which they turned back into very old humans and died.

**Finn, Benandonner, and the Giant's Causeway**
Finn is said to have built the Giant's Causeway, a formation of basalt columns in Northern Ireland, to reach the Scottish giant Benandonner. When the bigger giant came, Finn's wife Oonagh disguised Finn as a baby and served Benandonner a griddle cake with the iron griddle baked inside, while the "baby" ate an ordinary one. Terrified of how big the father must be, Benandonner fled and tore up the causeway behind him.

**Banshees, leprechauns, puca, and Saint Patrick**
Irish folklore includes the banshee, a female spirit whose wailing foretells a death and which is linked to the custom of keening (mourning cries) at funerals. It also includes the leprechaun, a fairy shoemaker with a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow, and the puca, a shape-shifter. Saint Patrick, who Christianized Ireland, is said to have driven out its snakes and explained the Trinity with a shamrock.
